blocks.text: There is, however, a remarkable disagreement among interpreters in explaining these words. To begin with the ancients, the Alexandrians render this verse as follows: Μυιαι θανατουσαι σαπριουσι σκευασιαν ἐλαιου ἡδύσματος· τίμιον ὀλίγον σοφιας ὑπὲρ δόξαν ἀφροσυνης μεγαλην [Myiai thanatousai sapriousi skeuasian elaiou hēdysmatos; timion oligon sophias hyper doxan aphrosynēs megalēn]. They omit the Hebrew יביע, which they seem not to have understood, just as they did not grasp the sense of the whole simile. Yet the Vulgate translator follows them, rendering: "Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment: wisdom and glory are more precious than a little and short-lived folly". Among the more recent interpreters ZIRKEL follows them too. He thinks that the first member of the verse (זבובי-רקח) should be referred to the preceding chapter, so that the words יקר — מעט form a new sentence, yielding the sense the Alexandrians express: a little wisdom is more precious than the glory of folly. Yet he could draw out this sense only by altering the Masoretic text [III, 345]: he places the word מעט before מחכמה, following the Alexandrians, who have ὀλίγον σοφίας [oligon sophias], and holds that this מעט מחכמה, which he himself formed, should be rendered word for word ὀλίγον ἀπὸ σοφίας [oligon apo sophias], which he declares to be the same in sense as ὀλίγον σοφίας [oligon sophias]. This interpretive device is hardly likely to win anyone else's approval. I. E. CHR. SCHMIDT also refers the first part of the verse to the preceding chapter, but renders the other member, יקר מחכמה מכבוד סכלות מעט, thus: more excellent than wisdom and honour is folly and poverty (Besser, als Weisheit und Ansehn, ist — Thorheit und Dürftigkeit). He says the sense of this paradox [παραδόξου (paradoxou)] is that it is better to be needy and to be thought a fool than to put on a show of wisdom in order to excite people's admiration. The chief objection to this interpretation is that מעט nowhere occurs with the meaning poverty. DOEDERLEIN departs from all of these. In his Scholia in Libros poeticos V. T. on this passage, with an interpretation that is certainly unusual and, as he himself says, bold, he renders our passage: He dries up deadly fluxes who opens springs of the perfumer's oil. He thinks the words יבאיש and יביע correspond to each other by way of antithesis: יביע is said of water bursting forth from springs, as in Prov. XV, 2. 28., while באש agrees in meaning with יבש, to be dry, in the fourth conjugation to make dry; זבובים are fluxes, from זוב to flow, and זבובי מות are deadly fluxes, wounds and ulcers, as כלי מות are deadly weapons and עץ מות a death-bringing tree. Opposed to these is שמן רוקח, the perfumer's oil, wholesome and refreshing. Hence the sense results: as he who pours out the perfumer's oil, whose great power in wounds is praised, dries up deadly fluxes, haemorrhages and the like, so a wise man who uses gentle words soothes and removes many harms. The last words he renders: glory through wisdom surpasses honour acquired by folly, even the least. You see that in this interpretation too new and unusual meanings are attached to the words, and the whole course of the discourse is altogether twisted in an extraordinary way. It will therefore be simplest to interpret our words in the way Bochart did above, or to follow the Syriac translator, the most learned of the ancient interpreters, who renders the first verse thus: ܐܝܟ ܕܒ̈ܒܐ ܕܡܝܬܝܢ ܡܣܪܚܝܢ ܠܡܐܢܐ ܕܡܫܚܐ ܒܣܝܡܐ. ܝܩܝܪܐ ܗܝ ܡܢ ܚܟܡܬܐ ܘܡܢ ܣܘܓܐܐ ܕܬܫܒܘܚܬܐ ܣܟܠܘܬܐ ܩܠܝܠܐ As dead flies make a vessel of sweet ointment stink, a little folly outweighs wisdom and much glory. He did, however, omit the verb יביע. But there will be no difficulty if you join the two, יבאיש יביע, so as to render the second, יביע, adverbially: makes it stink, belching forth, or ceaselessly, i.e. makes the stench bubble up or belch forth like gushing water. On this Hebraism see GLASSIUS, Philol. S. p. 272, ed. Dath. Similarly A. Schultens, in Commentar. ad Prov. XIII, 5. p. 122, renders our words: A dead fly makes the perfumer's balsam ferment with a stench and bubble up. By זבובי מות, however, I would understand deadly flies, or harmful ones, just as כלי מות, Ps. VII, 14. are deadly weapons.
